name: trader-alerts
description: >-
  Price Alerts. Rings when a price target, a stop or the opening bell hits:
  above / below / stop rules, percent moves from the previous close, and the
  NYSE opening bell, each ringing once so you are not spammed. Knows NYSE
  hours with the 2026 and 2027 holidays and 1:00 p.m. early closes, fetches
  free delayed quotes (Yahoo chart JSON, Stooq CSV) one ticker at a time, and
  writes trader/prices.json for the other skills. Use when the user says
  "alert me when", "tell me if AAPL hits", "set a stop", "price target",
  "watch my stocks", "is the market open", "when does the market open",
  "get me prices", or to refresh prices before sizing, risk or tax.
argument-hint: "[ticker] [price]"

# trader-alerts

Price Alerts watches the numbers so the user does not have to. An alert is
information, never an order: when a stop rings, nothing is sold. If the user
wants to act, the normal path runs (size, risk, their yes).

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" clock                         # NYSE open or closed, next open
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" quote AAPL KO --write         # -> trader/prices.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" quote --holdings --write      # portfolio + targets tickers
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --symbol AAPL --above 350
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --symbol BAC --stop 50 --note "my stop"
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --symbol KO --pct 3
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" add --opening-bell
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" check                         # exit 0 = something rang
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" list
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/alerts.py" reset aapl-above-350
```

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/alerts.json` | the rules (`alerts.example.json` in this folder) |
| `trader/state/alerts.json` | which rules rang and when, so each rings once |
| `trader/prices.json` | the latest quotes, merged in, for trader-budget, trader-risk, trader-tax and trader-rebalance |

## Rule types

| type | rings when | rings again |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `above` | price at or above `price` | after `reset`, or on its own if `"rearm": true` and the price fell back |
| `below` / `stop` | price at or below `price` | same |
| `pct_move` | moved `pct` percent from the previous close (or `ref`), optional `direction` up or down | once per day at most |
| `opening_bell` | the NYSE is open | once per trading day |

## Quotes

- `yahoo` (default): `query1.finance.yahoo.com/v8/finance/chart/<TICKER>`, an
  unofficial free JSON endpoint, one request per ticker, half a second apart.
- `stooq`: `stooq.com/q/l/?s=aapl.us&f=sd2t2ohlcv&h&e=csv`, Stooq's free CSV.
  It answered 404 when this was written (2026-10-13); the parser stays for
  when it is back. Use `--source stooq` to try it.
- Free quotes are delayed. They are fine for alerts and for checking sizes,
  not for timing an order. The broker's price is the one that fills.
- If both are down, read prices from the broker connector (Alpaca
  `get_stock_snapshot`, IBKR `get_price_snapshot`) and write them into
  `trader/prices.json` as `{"as_of": "...", "prices": {"AAPL": 341.27}}`.

## The NYSE clock

Regular session 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. New York time, closed on weekends and
on these holidays, from nyse.com/markets/hours-calendars (read 2026-10-13):

- 2026: Jan 1, Jan 19, Feb 16, Apr 3 (Good Friday), May 25, Jun 19, Jul 3
  (Independence Day observed), Sep 7, Nov 26, Dec 25. Early close 1:00 p.m. on
  Nov 27 and Dec 24.
- 2027: Jan 1, Jan 18, Feb 15, Mar 26 (Good Friday), May 31, Jun 18
  (Juneteenth observed), Jul 5 (Independence Day observed), Sep 6, Nov 25,
  Dec 24 (Christmas observed). Early close 1:00 p.m. on Nov 26.

Daylight saving time is worked out in the tool, so it needs no time zone
files. For any other year it says the holiday list is unknown.

## Steps

1. Ask what to watch, in the user's words ("tell me if Apple drops under
   $320"), and add the rule. Confirm it back: ticker, type, level.
2. Run `check` now, and on a schedule if the user wants (a Claude scheduled
   task or cron, every 15 minutes in market hours is plenty). Each run fetches
   only the tickers in the rules and rings each alert once.
3. Tell the user what rang in one line each. If they want to act, send them
   to sizing and `/trader-risk`. Never act for them.

## Example: the reel's portfolio

After the copy portfolio is bought, `add --opening-bell`, `add --symbol AAPL
--above 350`, and `add --symbol BAC --stop 50`. On 2026-10-13 AAPL closed at
$341.27 and BAC at $53.96, so `check` that evening prints "Nothing hit" and
exits 1. At 9:30 the next morning the opening bell rings once.

## What it never does

It never places, cancels or changes an order, never claims a quote is
real time, and never predicts where a price is going.

## Safety

- Education and tooling, not financial advice. An alert is a fact about a price, not a signal to trade.
- Paper trading by default (`"paper": true`). Going live is the user's own decision, in their own config.
- Nothing in this pack places an order except trader-broker, and only when all three hold: trader-risk
  passed that exact order today, the user typed an explicit yes for that one order in the chat, and the
  user clicked Allow once on Claude's own card because the order tool is set to "Needs approval"
  (Customize > Connectors > tool permissions). Never set an order tool to "Always allow".
- No options, margin, short selling or leverage unless the config allows it and the user confirms.
- Broker keys live in environment variables or the Claude Desktop config, never in the chat.

# trader-analyst

Earnings season moves stocks, and the press release is written to put the
best number first. This skill reads the numbers the company actually filed
with the SEC, lines them up quarter by quarter, and says plainly what changed.

Tool in this folder (standard library Python, no keys):

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/facts.py" --help
```

It needs the SEC User-Agent (`sec_user_agent` in `trader/config.json`, or
`SEC_USER_AGENT`): "Your Name you@example.com" with the user's real name and
email. It refuses to call SEC without one.

## What it reads and writes

- Reads `https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK##########.json` (every
  number the company has tagged in its filings), the company's submissions
  list (for the newest 10-Q or 10-K and the newest 8-K with item 2.02,
  "Results of Operations") and that 8-K's folder to find the press release
  (the EX-99.1 exhibit).
- Writes `trader/metrics.json` with `--metrics`: one row per company (TTM
  revenue, net income and diluted EPS, the latest margins and growth) for
  `/trader-screener`. `metrics.example.json` in this folder is a real run
  for AAPL, AXP, GOOGL, KO and BAC on 2026-10-13.

## The rules

- **Filed numbers first.** The table comes from XBRL facts the company filed.
  Use the press release for context (guidance, segment colour), and say which
  numbers came from where.
- **Compare like with like.** Growth is against the same quarter a year
  earlier. Quarter-on-quarter changes are shown but many businesses are
  seasonal (Apple's December quarter is always its biggest).
- **Say what is derived.** Companies do not file a Q4 10-Q. The fourth
  quarter is the 10-K year minus the three quarters inside it and is marked
  "derived"; derived EPS is approximate.
- **Say when the data lags.** SEC's facts API can trail a filing. When the
  newest 10-Q is later than the newest quarter in the facts, the tool prints a
  NOTE with the link: read the 10-Q itself before summarising.
- **Flag one-offs.** When net income is above operating income, gains outside
  the business (investment marks, tax items) are inside it. The tool says so.
  Banks and insurers have no gross margin: blank, not zero.

## Steps

1. Run it for the companies in question (or every ticker in
   `trader/targets.json`):

   ```bash
   python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/facts.py" AAPL
   python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/facts.py" AAPL AXP GOOGL KO BAC --metrics trader/metrics.json
   ```

   `--quarters 8` shows two years, `--json` everything machine-readable,
   `--cik` a company without a ticker.
2. Open the latest earnings press release (the EX-99 link) and the 10-Q when
   the numbers need context, and read them.
3. Write the summary: one line on the quarter (revenue, EPS, growth), one on
   margins, one on anything unusual (a one-off, a derived quarter, data that
   lags), and the links. Plain words, real numbers, no adjectives the numbers
   do not support.

## Example: the reel's top holding

`facts.py AAPL` (2026-10-13): quarter ending 2026-06-27 (fiscal Q3 2026),
revenue $109.42B, +16.4% against a year earlier, net income $29.79B (+27.1%),
diluted EPS $2.02 (+28.7%); gross margin 50.1% (+0.8 points on the quarter
before); last four quarters $466.8B revenue and $8.71 EPS. Press release:
the EX-99.1 of the 8-K filed 2026-07-30. For Coca-Cola the tool notes that
SEC's facts stop at 2026-04-03 while the 10-Q for 2026-07-03 is already filed,
so the summary reads that 10-Q directly.

## What it never does

- Never says a stock is cheap, expensive, a buy or a sell. It reports what
  the company filed.
- Never invents a number the filings do not have, or estimates a quarter it
  cannot derive.
- Never calls SEC without the User-Agent, and stays well under 10 requests a
  second.

## Safety

Education and tooling, not financial advice. This skill only reads filings.
Nothing places an order except `/trader-broker`, after `/trader-risk` passes
and the user types an explicit yes for that order.

# trader-broker

The Order Executor is the only skill in this pack that can lead to a real
order, so it is the strictest. An order reaches the market only after three
separate gates, every time, for every order:

1. **trader-risk passed this exact order today** (matched by fingerprint).
2. **The user typed an explicit yes for this one order** in the chat.
3. **The user clicked Allow once** on Claude's own permission card, which
   appears because the order tool is set to "Needs approval".

Two yeses from the user, one PASS from the rules. No yes, no order.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" show                     # every ticket, READY or not
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" approve --index 1 --reply "yes"
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" result --index 1 --status placed --broker-id ID
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" fill --symbol AAPL --side buy --qty 3.6628 --price 341.27
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ticket.py" log
```

`ticket.py` never talks to a broker. It renders tickets, checks that a reply
is a real yes for that order, and keeps the log in `trader/state/broker.json`.

## Setup A: Alpaca (official MCP server, Claude Desktop)

Alpaca's own server is github.com/alpacahq/alpaca-mcp-server (MIT). It runs on
the user's computer inside Claude Desktop. It is not in Claude's connector
directory. It trades on a **paper** account unless told otherwise.

1. The user makes an Alpaca account and creates **paper trading** API keys in
   the Alpaca dashboard. Paper keys are separate from live keys.
2. The user installs `uv` (it provides `uvx`), from docs.astral.sh/uv.
3. In Claude Desktop: Settings > Developer > Edit Config. That opens
   `claude_desktop_config.json` (macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/`,
   Windows: `%APPDATA%\Claude\`). The user adds this block (also in
   `claude_desktop_config.example.json` here) and types their own keys into the file:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "alpaca": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["alpaca-mcp-server"],
      "env": {
        "ALPACA_API_KEY": "paste your paper key here, in this file only",
        "ALPACA_SECRET_KEY": "paste your paper secret here, in this file only",
        "ALPACA_PAPER_TRADE": "true",
        "ALPACA_TOOLSETS": "account,trading,stock-data"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

   The `env` block hands the keys to the server as environment variables.
   **Keys never go in the chat.** Never ask for them, never read this file
   back into the conversation, and if the user pastes a key anyway, tell them
   to delete that message and make new keys in the Alpaca dashboard.
   `ALPACA_PAPER_TRADE` is already true by default; writing it makes it
   visible. `ALPACA_TOOLSETS` is optional and hides the tools they do not need.
4. Restart Claude Desktop.
5. **Set the tool permissions.** Customize > Connectors (Settings > Connectors
   in older versions), open alpaca, and for each tool pick Always allow, Needs
   approval or Blocked:
   - `place_stock_order`: **Needs approval**. Never Always allow.
   - every other tool that places, changes, cancels or closes anything
     (`cancel_order_by_id`, `close_position`, `update_account_config`): Needs approval.
   - `place_option_order`, `place_crypto_order`, `close_all_positions`,
     `cancel_all_orders`, `exercise_options_position`: **Blocked** unless the
     user has a reason and says so.
   - read-only tools (`get_account_info`, `get_all_positions`, `get_stock_snapshot`,
     `get_stock_latest_quote`): Always allow is fine.

# trader-budget

The Budget Manager turns "copy this portfolio" into "buy exactly this much of
each", inside rules the user sets once. It writes proposals only. trader-risk
checks them and trader-broker asks the user yes or no for each one.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py"                       # trader/targets.json + trader/config.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py" --budget 5000 --write # write trader/orders.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py" --whole-shares --prices trader/prices.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py" --weights AAPL=22.04,AXP=17.14,GOOGL=12.62 --json
```

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/config.json` | the rules (start from `config.example.json` in this folder) |
| `trader/targets.json` | the weights to copy, written by trader-copycat (`targets.example.json` here) |
| `trader/prices.json` | only for whole shares or share counts (trader-alerts writes it) |
| `trader/orders.json` | the proposed buy orders it writes with `--write` |

## Step 1: set the rules once

If `trader/config.json` does not exist, copy `config.example.json` into
`trader/config.json` and ask the user for each value in plain words:

- **budget**: how much money this is for. Only money they can afford to lose.
- **cash_buffer_pct**: how much stays in cash (default 10).
- **max_position_pct**: the most any one stock may be, as a percent of the budget (default 25).
- **max_order_usd** and **min_order_usd**: the biggest and smallest single order (2000 and 5).
- **fractional**: true if the broker buys fractional shares (Alpaca does); false for whole shares.
- **blocked**: tickers they never want to own.
- Keep **paper** true until they have watched it work on a paper account.

## Step 2: size it

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/size.py" --write
```

The maths, in order: the cash buffer comes off the top; the weights are
renormalised to 100 over the stocks that are left; any stock over the cap is
pinned at the cap and its excess is shared over the others by weight, again
until nobody is over; a slice under the minimum order is dropped and its
weight shared out; amounts are rounded to whole dollars and the rounding
dollar goes to the biggest stock that is not capped, so nothing is left
idle by accident. Money that truly cannot be invested (every stock at its
cap, or whole shares that do not divide evenly) is shown as "left idle".

## Step 3: show the user

Show the table: ticker, weight, dollars, which stock hit the cap, the cash
buffer and what is left idle. Say where the weights came from and how old
they are (a 13F is up to 45 days old when it is filed). Then hand over to
`/trader-risk`.

## Example: the reel

Berkshire Hathaway's Q2 2026 13F (filed 2026-08-14), top five: Apple 22.04%,
American Express 17.14%, Alphabet 12.62%, Coca-Cola 10.86%, Bank of America
9.20%. Renormalised over those five: 30.67 / 23.85 / 17.56 / 15.11 / 12.80.
A $5,000 budget, a 10% cash buffer and a 25% cap:

| stock | dollars | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AAPL | $1,250 | capped at 25% |
| AXP | $1,119 | |
| GOOGL | $823 | |
| KO | $708 | |
| BAC | $600 | |
| cash buffer | $500 | |
| left idle | $0 | |

The first order it writes is
`{"symbol": "AAPL", "side": "buy", "notional": "1250", "type": "market", "time_in_force": "day"}`.
Keep the weights to two decimals or more: weights already rounded to one
decimal (30.7 / 23.9 / ...) can move a slice by a dollar.

## Rules

- Proposals only. This skill never calls a broker tool.
- Never size money the user has not said is for this. Ask for the budget.
- Every number comes from the config, the targets or the prices. Nothing is guessed.
- No projections: never say what the positions will be worth or earn.
- Whole shares need real prices from `trader/prices.json`; never invent a price.

## What it never does

It never places, approves or schedules an order, never raises a limit on its
own, and never sizes options, margin or short positions.

# trader-copycat

Copying an investor starts with what they are legally required to show: a
13F-HR, filed with the SEC every quarter by any investment manager with over
$100 million in US-listed stocks and other 13(f) securities. This skill reads
it straight from SEC EDGAR, rebuilds the portfolio, and turns it into target
weights for your own account.

Tool in this folder (standard library Python, no keys):

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/edgar13f.py" --help
```

SEC asks every program to identify itself with a name and email. Set it once
in `trader/config.json` (`"sec_user_agent": "Your Name you@example.com"`, with
the user's real name and email) or `export SEC_USER_AGENT=...`. The tool
refuses to call SEC without it and says how to fix it. Ask the user for it;
never invent one.

## What it writes

- `trader/targets.json`: the weights to copy, in the shape every other trader
  skill reads: `{ "source", "as_of", "weights": [ {"ticker", "name",
  "weight"} ] }`, weights in % with 2 decimals summing to 100 over the stock
  sleeve (keep the 2 decimals: budget sizing needs them), plus the
  13F share, value, CUSIPs, what was skipped and why, and the caveats.
- `trader/tickers.json` (optional, yours): CUSIP to ticker fixes the tool
  will always use first, as `{"650111107": "NYT"}`.

`targets.example.json` in this folder is the real output of the reel's run
(Berkshire, top 5).

## The rules

- **Say how old the data is, every time.** A 13F is a snapshot of the last
  day of the quarter, filed up to 45 days later. Say "holdings as of
  2026-06-30, filed 2026-08-14" in every answer that uses one.
- **Say what it cannot show.** Long US-listed positions only: no shorts, no
  cash, no bonds, no foreign shares, no private companies, nothing bought and
  sold inside the quarter, and no prices paid.
- **The firm, not the person.** Berkshire Hathaway files the 13F, not Warren
  Buffett. Greg Abel has been CEO since 2026-01-01 and Buffett became
  Chairman Emeritus on 2026-09-18. Never say "Buffett bought" when the filing
  only says "Berkshire held".
- **Every number comes from the filing.** Quote the accession number and link
  the information table. If a ticker is a guess (marked `*`), say so and fix
  it with `--figi` or `trader/tickers.json` before anything is copied.
- **Options and bonds are never copied.** PUT, CALL and PRN rows are listed as
  excluded. This pack trades stocks only unless the config allows more.

## Step 1: find the investor

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/edgar13f.py" find buffett
```

# trader-news

A position you hold can change in a minute: an earnings miss, a CEO leaving,
a lawsuit, a restatement. This skill reads the two feeds that carry those
first for each of your stocks and tells you only what is new.

Tool in this folder (standard library Python, no keys):

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/news.py" --help
```

## What it reads and writes

- Your tickers: `--tickers`, else `trader/portfolio.json` positions, else
  `trader/targets.json` weights (so it works right after `/trader-copycat`).
- Headlines: Yahoo Finance's public headline RSS, one feed per ticker
  (`https://feeds.finance.yahoo.com/rss/2.0/headline?s=AAPL&region=US&lang=en-US`).
- Filings: SEC EDGAR's company Atom feed, 8-K by default (`--forms 8-K,10-Q`
  for more). Needs the SEC User-Agent from `trader/config.json`
  (`sec_user_agent`) or `SEC_USER_AGENT`. Without it, filings are skipped with
  a note and headlines still run.
- Writes `trader/state/news.json`: what has been shown (kept 30 days) and the
  CIK for each ticker, so every item appears once.

## The rules

- **Headlines are leads, not facts.** Before telling the user something
  happened, open the story or the filing and read it. Quote the source and
  link it. Never summarise a paywalled story you could not read: say it is
  paywalled.
- **Filings beat headlines.** If an 8-K and a headline disagree, the 8-K is
  what the company told the SEC.
- **Say what it touches.** Every item lists the tickers it touches (the feed
  it came from plus any of your tickers or company names it mentions) and
  tags (earnings, analyst, legal, deal, capital, people, risk). Filings marked
  `!` carry an important 8-K item: earnings results (2.02), an officer change
  (5.02), an impairment (2.06), a delisting notice (3.01), past financials no
  longer reliable (4.02), bankruptcy (1.03) or a cyber incident (1.05).
- **No predictions.** Report what was published. Never say what the stock
  will do next.

## Steps

1. Run the check:

   ```bash
   python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/news.py"
   python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/news.py" --tickers AAPL AXP GOOGL KO BAC --hours 24
   ```

   Exit code 1 means nothing new. `--all` shows items already seen,
   `--json` gives everything machine-readable, `--dry-run` leaves the state
   alone.
2. Read the items that matter: every `!` filing, every item tagged earnings,
   legal or risk, and anything touching the biggest positions first.
3. Write a short brief: per ticker, what happened, the source and link, and
   one line on why it matters to this portfolio (its weight, from
   `trader/targets.json` or `trader/portfolio.json`).
4. If a story might change the plan (an 8-K 4.02 restatement, a delisting
   notice), say so and suggest `/trader-analyst` for the numbers or
   `/trader-risk` to recheck pending orders. Never act on a headline alone.

To run it on a schedule, use `/loop 30m /trader-news` during market hours or
a scheduled task each morning.

## Example: the reel's portfolio

The user copied Berkshire's top 5 (AAPL, AXP, GOOGL, KO, BAC). On Tuesday
2026-10-13 the check shows Apple headlines first ("Apple Introduces HomeView
Smart Home Hub, Other Gadgets", "Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring
records in Apple trade secrets case", tagged legal), Coca-Cola dividend
pieces, and from SEC: Apple's 8-K of 2026-07-30 (item 2.02, earnings results)
and Coca-Cola's of 2026-07-28 (2.02). Brief: "Apple (your biggest position,
30.7%) launched a $299 smart home hub; a court ruling in its trade secrets
case against OpenAI. No new filings from your five companies this week." When
a ticker has no news, say so rather than padding the brief.

## What it never does

- Never invents or embellishes a story, a quote or a number.
- Never trades on news, and never tells the user to buy or sell because of a
  headline.
- Never hammers a server: one request per feed per ticker, a pause between
  SEC calls, and SEC's 10 requests a second limit stays far away.

## Safety

Education and tooling, not financial advice. This skill only reads and
reports. Nothing places an order except `/trader-broker`, after
`/trader-risk` passes and the user types an explicit yes for that order.

# trader-pelosi

Members of Congress have to report their trades, their spouse's and their
dependent children's. The House Clerk posts every report as a PDF and lists
them all in one index file per year. This skill reads that index, notices the
moment a new report appears, and reads the report for you.

It is fast. It is not early. A PTR is due within 30 days of the member
learning of the trade and never more than 45 days after it, so by the time
anyone can read it the trade is days or weeks old. There is no inside
information here: only public filings, read quickly. Say that every time.

Tool in this folder (standard library Python; `pdftotext` from poppler is
optional, to read the PDFs locally):

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" --help
```

## What it reads and writes

- Reads `https://disclosures-clerk.house.gov/public_disc/financial-pdfs/<YEAR>FD.zip`
  (one `<Member>` per filing: name, district, FilingType, FilingDate, DocID)
  and each PTR at `.../public_disc/ptr-pdfs/<YEAR>/<DocID>.pdf`.
- Writes `trader/state/pelosi.json` (the DocIDs already shown, so each PTR
  alerts once) and keeps downloaded PDFs in `trader/state/ptr-pdfs/`.
- Reads `trader/portfolio.json` (if it exists) to flag trades in what you hold.

## The rules

- **Quote the filing, not a tracker.** Every row comes from the PTR PDF on the
  Clerk's site, with its DocID and link. Third-party trackers are fine for
  browsing but can be off (Capitol Trades showed Pelosi's trade dates one day
  earlier than her PTRs). The PTR wins.
- **Amounts are ranges.** "$1,000,001 - $5,000,000", never "$3 million".
- **Owner matters.** SP is the spouse, JT joint, DC a dependent child, blank
  the member. Pelosi's 2026 trades are all SP: Paul Pelosi.
- **Say the delay.** Each row shows how many days passed between the trade
  and the filing; over 45 is flagged as late.
- **Options are options.** A call bought with a strike and an expiry is not
  a share purchase. The tool reads contracts, strike and expiry from the
  description and marks exercises.

## Step 1: what has been filed

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" index --member pelosi
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" index --since 2026-10-01        # every member
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" index --member "Josh Gottheimer" --year 2025
```

`--member` takes a last name, "First Last" or "Last, First", and repeats.
`--type ''` lists every filing type (annual reports are type O).

## Step 2: watch for new ones

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" new --member pelosi --read
```

Shows only PTRs not seen at the last check (the first run shows the last 45
days), downloads and reads them with `--read`, and records them in the state
file. Exit code 1 means nothing new. In January it also checks last year's
index. The Clerk rebuilds the index file about once a day (the copy read on
2026-10-13 was stamped 09:00 that morning), so checking every hour on weekdays
is plenty: run it with `/loop 1h` or a scheduled task.

## Step 3: read a report

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" fetch 20035143
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/ptr.py" parse ptr.txt --filed 2026-08-21 --json
```

`fetch` saves the PDF and, if `pdftotext` is installed, prints the rows. If it
is not installed, open the saved PDF and read it directly: you can read PDFs.
`parse` turns `pdftotext -layout` text into rows. Check the row count against
the PDF when a report runs over several pages.

## Example: the reel's alert

```
NEW Periodic Transaction Report: Hon. Nancy Pelosi (CA11) filed 2026-08-21, doc 20035143
```

  skips tiny trades, lists sells before buys, and writes the trades to

# trader-rebalance

The Rebalancer keeps the portfolio looking like the plan. Prices move, new
money arrives and a new 13F changes the weights; this skill finds the stocks
that drifted too far and proposes the trades that bring them back. It writes
proposals only: trader-risk checks them and trader-broker asks the user yes
or no for each one.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/rebalance.py"                    # the drift table, no files written
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/rebalance.py" --band 5 --write   # proposals -> trader/orders.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/rebalance.py" --sell-untracked   # also sell holdings not in the targets
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/rebalance.py" --json
```

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/portfolio.json` | cash and positions (shares); same shape as trader-tax's `portfolio.example.json` |
| `trader/prices.json` | a price for every holding and every target (trader-alerts writes it) |
| `trader/targets.json` | the target weights (trader-copycat writes it) |
| `trader/config.json` | cash buffer, cap, min and max order, `rebalance_band_pct` |
| `trader/orders.json` | the proposals it writes with `--write`, sells first |

## How it decides

- **Account value** = cash + every holding at its price.
- **Targets**: the weights renormalised over the stock sleeve (account minus
  the cash buffer), with no stock above `max_position_pct` of the account. The
  excess is shared out, the same way trader-budget does it, so a capped stock
  is not bought back over the cap every month.
- **Drift** = current percent of the account minus target percent.
- **Band**: only stocks drifting MORE than the band trade (default 5 points).
  A trade takes the stock all the way back to its target. A small band means
  more trades; a wide band means fewer.
- **Sells first**, then buys. Buys only spend cash above the buffer; if there
  is not enough, all buys are scaled down by the same share.
- Trades under `min_order_usd` are skipped. A trade over `max_order_usd` is
  cut to the max with a note to run again after it fills.
- **Untracked** holdings (not in the targets) are left alone and listed,
  unless the user asks to sell them with `--sell-untracked`.

## Steps

1. Refresh prices: trader-alerts `alerts.py quote --holdings --write`.
2. Run `rebalance.py` and show the drift table in plain words: which stocks
   are over or under, by how many points, and what it would trade.
3. Before any sell, run trader-tax (`lots.py sell TICKER SHARES`) and show
   what the sale would realize. Selling a winner can mean a tax bill.
4. If the user wants the trades: `rebalance.py --write`, then `/trader-risk`,
   then `/trader-broker`, one yes per order.

## Example: the reel's portfolio

The copy portfolio bought on 2026-10-13 (AAPL $1,250 capped, AXP $1,119,
GOOGL $823, KO $708, BAC $600, $500 cash), valued at that day's closes, sits
on its targets: every drift is under 0.1 point, so `rebalance.py` says
"Nothing is outside the band" and exits 1. If the user adds $2,000 of cash,
the account is $7,000 and the cap becomes $1,750. AAPL is now 7.1 points under
its target and AXP 6.4, both outside the 5-point band, so it proposes buying
$499 of AAPL and $446 of AXP. GOOGL, KO and BAC are under target too, but
inside the band, so they wait. Add $5,000 instead and all five are outside
the band: five buys that leave the $1,000 buffer in cash.

## What it never does

It never places an order, never trades inside the band to chase small
differences, never sells holdings outside the targets unless asked, and
never says a rebalance will improve returns.

## Safety

- Education and tooling, not financial advice. A rebalance follows the user's own targets, not a forecast.
- Paper trading by default (`"paper": true`). Going live is the user's own decision, in their own config.
- Nothing in this pack places an order except trader-broker, and only when all three hold: trader-risk
  passed that exact order today, the user typed an explicit yes for that one order in the chat, and the
  user clicked Allow once on Claude's own card because the order tool is set to "Needs approval"
  (Customize > Connectors > tool permissions). Never set an order tool to "Always allow".
- No options, margin, short selling or leverage unless the config allows it and the user confirms.
- Broker keys live in environment variables or the Claude Desktop config, never in the chat.

# trader-risk

The Risk Manager is the gate between a proposal and the broker. Every order
written by trader-budget, trader-rebalance or trader-tax passes through it.
A BLOCK is final for that order: it does not go to the user for a yes, and
it does not go to the broker.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/check.py"             # trader/ files; writes trader/state/risk.json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/check.py" --json
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/check.py" --no-write  # look without recording
```

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/orders.json` | the proposed orders |
| `trader/config.json` | the limits (trader-budget ships `config.example.json`) |
| `trader/portfolio.json` | cash and holdings; if missing, a fresh account funded with the budget |
| `trader/prices.json` | needed to size share-count orders and value holdings |
| `trader/state/broker.json` | what was placed today, for duplicates and the daily limit |
| `trader/state/risk.json` | the verdicts it writes, with a fingerprint of each exact order |

## The checks

Orders are checked in file order, as if each passed order had filled, so a
batch that is fine order by order but breaks a rule together is caught.

| check | blocks when |
| --- | --- |
| format | no symbol, side not buy or sell, both or neither of qty and notional, a notional order that is not market + day (Alpaca's rule), a limit order with no limit price |
| asset | an option symbol while `allow_options` is false; crypto or anything that is not a US stock or ETF ticker |
| blocked | the ticker is on the `blocked` list |
| size | under `min_order_usd` or over `max_order_usd` |
| position | the stock would be over `max_position_pct` of the account after the fill |
| cash | the buy would leave less than the cash buffer, or need margin (`allow_margin` false) |
| short | a sell of more than you hold (`allow_short` false) |
| duplicate | the same symbol and side twice in one batch, or already placed today |
| daily limit | more than `max_orders_per_day` placed today |

Warnings do not block, but say them to the user: a LIVE account, a number
sent as a number instead of a string, an advanced (bracket) order.

## Steps

1. Make sure `trader/prices.json` is fresh if any order is a share count or
   any holding needs a value (trader-alerts: `alerts.py quote --holdings --write`).
2. Run `check.py`. Exit code 0 means every order passed, 1 means at least one
   was blocked.
3. Tell the user the result in plain words, order by order. For a BLOCK, give
   the reason and the fix (a smaller amount, a different stock, or a rule the
   user may decide to change). Never change a limit yourself.
4. If the orders change in any way, run the check again. trader-broker matches
   each order to its verdict by fingerprint, so an edited order is not ready
   until it passes again, and a verdict from yesterday does not count today.

## Example: the reel

The five buys from trader-budget (AAPL $1,250, AXP $1,119, GOOGL $823, KO
$708, BAC $600) on a fresh $5,000 paper account with the example config:

```
PASS  #1 buy AAPL $1,250
PASS  #2 buy AXP $1,119
PASS  #3 buy GOOGL $823
PASS  #4 buy KO $708
PASS  #5 buy BAC $600
5 passed, 0 blocked. Cash after the passed orders: $500 (paper account).
```

AAPL lands exactly on the 25% cap ($1,250 of $5,000), which is allowed. A
sixth order, another $100 of AAPL, is blocked three ways: it would dip into
the $500 cash buffer, put AAPL over its 25% cap, and repeat AAPL in the same
batch.

## What it never does

It never places an order, never edits an order to make it pass, never
loosens a limit, and never treats a PASS as the user's yes. A PASS only means
the order is allowed to be shown to the user.

# trader-screener

A screen turns "I want profitable companies that are still growing and not
too expensive" into rules a computer can check, and shows its work: every
pass and every fail comes with the number and the threshold.

Tool in this folder (standard library Python, no network):

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/screen.py" --help
```

## What it reads and writes

- Metrics: `trader/metrics.json` from `/trader-analyst` (`facts.py --metrics`),
  or any JSON list or CSV with a `ticker` column. CSV numbers may carry `$`,
  `%` and commas.
- Prices (optional): `trader/prices.json` (`{"prices": {"AAPL": 341.27}}`,
  any source; `/trader-alerts` writes it). With prices it adds `price`, `pe`
  (price / trailing EPS, only when EPS is positive) and `earnings_yield`.
- Rules: a JSON file, `rules.example.json` in this folder to start from.
- Writes `trader/shortlist.json` with `--out`: who passed, their score and
  why, who failed and why.

## The rules file

```json
{"name": "Growing, profitable, not priced for perfection",
 "rules": [{"metric": "revenue_growth_yoy", "op": ">=", "value": 10},
           {"metric": "operating_margin", "op": ">=", "value": 25},
           {"metric": "pe", "op": "<=", "value": 35}],
 "rank":  [{"metric": "revenue_growth_yoy", "order": "desc", "weight": 2},
           {"metric": "pe", "order": "asc", "weight": 1}],
 "missing": "fail"}
```

Ops: `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `==`, `!=`, `between` ([low, high]), `in` and
`not in` (a list, for tickers or sectors to leave out). `"missing": "fail"`
fails a company that lacks a metric a rule needs (banks have no operating
margin in SEC's facts); `"skip"` ignores that rule for it and says so.
Ranking scores each passing company 0 to 1 per rank metric and takes the
weighted average.

## Steps

1. Turn the user's words into rules. Ask when a threshold is vague ("cheap"
   means what P/E?). Write them to `trader/rules.json`.
2. Get metrics for the candidates: run `/trader-analyst` on them with
   `--metrics trader/metrics.json` (its `facts.py AAPL AXP GOOGL KO BAC
   --metrics trader/metrics.json`), or use the user's own CSV. Prices from
   `trader/prices.json` if P/E matters.
3. Run the screen:

   ```bash
   python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/screen.py" trader/metrics.json --rules trader/rules.json \
     --prices trader/prices.json --out trader/shortlist.json
   ```

   Exit code 1 means nothing passed: say so and show the closest misses.
4. Report the shortlist with the reasons, the misses with the numbers that
   failed, and the dates the numbers are from (the latest quarter end per
   company, the price date). Suggest `/trader-analyst` on the top names before
   anything else.

## Example: the reel's five

Metrics from SEC for AAPL, AXP, GOOGL, KO and BAC, prices at the 2026-10-13
close, and `rules.example.json`:

```
Growing, profitable, not priced for perfection: 2 of 5 companies pass.
 1. PASS GOOGL  Alphabet Inc.  score 0.75   (growth 24.2, P/E 17.8)
 2. PASS KO     COCA COLA CO   score 0.25   (growth 12.1, P/E 28.3)
    FAIL AAPL   pe 39.2, needs <= 35
    FAIL BAC    operating_margin is missing
    FAIL AXP    revenue_growth_yoy 8.6, needs >= 10; operating_margin is missing
```

Then the caveats a careful analyst adds: Alphabet's latest quarter has net
income above operating income (gains outside the business), and Coca-Cola's
numbers stop at the quarter ending 2026-04-03 because SEC's facts lag its
latest 10-Q.

## What it never does

- Never calls a passing company a buy. A screen is a filter on reported
  numbers, not a recommendation.
- Never fills in a missing number or guesses a metric: missing means missing.
- Never sends anything to `/trader-budget` or an order path by itself.

## Safety

Education and tooling, not financial advice. This skill only filters numbers.
Nothing places an order except `/trader-broker`, after `/trader-risk` passes
and the user types an explicit yes for that order.

# trader-tax

The Tax Optimizer does the arithmetic on the user's lots so nobody sells
blind. It never decides what is right for the user's taxes. **This is not tax
advice**: a tax professional decides what applies to them. Say that once,
early, in every answer that uses this skill.

`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` below is this skill's folder (where this SKILL.md lives).

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/lots.py" report --lots              # every lot, gain or loss, term
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/lots.py" sell KO 2 --price 90.11    # what a sale would realize (FIFO)
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/lots.py" sell KO 2 --method specific --lots KO-2
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/lots.py" harvest --min-loss 100     # candidates, with wash-sale checks
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/lots.py" harvest --min-loss 100 --write
python3 "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/lots.py" wash KO                    # is buying KO today a wash sale?
```

## What it reads and writes

| file | what |
| --- | --- |
| `trader/portfolio.json` | positions with lots: `{"id", "date", "shares", "cost"}` (cost = total basis); shape: `portfolio.example.json` here |
| `trader/prices.json` | current prices (trader-alerts: `alerts.py quote --holdings --write`) |
| `trader/orders.json` | planned buys count for wash sales; `harvest --write` replaces it with sell proposals |
| `trader/state/tax.json` | the realized sales it logs with `sell --record` |

Lots come from the fills trader-broker records (`ticket.py fill`), or from the
user's broker statement. If a position has shares but no lots, ask for the
purchase dates and costs. Never invent a cost basis.

## The rules it applies (US federal, arithmetic only)

- **Term**: long term if sold more than one year after the purchase date,
  otherwise short term. `report --lots` shows the date each lot turns long term.
- **Lot methods**: `fifo` (oldest first, what most brokers do by default),
  `hifo` (highest cost first) and `specific` (named lots). The order sent to
  the broker does not carry lot ids: to sell specific lots the user must
  choose them in the broker's own tax-lot setting, or the broker uses its
  default method.
- **Wash sale**: a loss is disallowed to the extent the same or a
  substantially identical stock is bought within 30 days before or after the
  sale. The tool checks the other lots still held, planned buys in
  `trader/orders.json` and the loss sales it has logged. It cannot see an IRA,
  a spouse's account or another broker, and those count too. Say so.

## Steps

1. Refresh prices, then `lots.py report --lots`. Show gains and losses by
   stock, and which lots are short or long term.
2. Before any sell (rebalance, a stop, a change of mind), run `lots.py sell`
   with the planned shares and method and show what it would realize.
3. For harvesting: `lots.py harvest --min-loss 100` (and `--min-pct` if the
   user wants a percent threshold). For each candidate show the estimated
   loss, short and long term split, any wash-sale conflict, and the first day
   they could buy it back. Candidates with a conflict are not proposed.
4. Only if the user wants proposals: `harvest --write`, then `/trader-risk`,
   then `/trader-broker`, one yes per order.
5. After a sale fills, `lots.py sell ... --record` updates the lots and logs
   the realized result for the year.

## Example: the reel's portfolio

The copy portfolio bought on 2026-10-13 (AAPL $1,250, AXP $1,119, GOOGL $823,
KO $708, BAC $600) has one lot per stock, all short term until 2027-10-14.
If BAC later trades below its $600 basis, `harvest --min-loss 25` lists the
BAC-1 lot with its loss and "do not buy BAC again before" a date 31 days
after the sale. If the user also has a BAC buy planned in `trader/orders.json`,
it flags a wash sale instead of proposing the sell.

## What it never does

It never files anything, never gives a tax rate or a tax bill, never tells
the user what they owe, never places an order, and never proposes a harvest
that it can see would be a wash sale.

## Safety

- Not tax advice, and education and tooling, not financial advice. Check with a tax professional.
- Paper trading by default (`"paper": true`). Going live is the user's own decision, in their own config.
- Nothing in this pack places an order except trader-broker, and only when all three hold: trader-risk

  user clicked Allow once on Claude's own card because the order tool is set to "Needs approval"
  (Customize > Connectors > tool permissions). Never set an order tool to "Always allow".
- No options, margin, short selling or leverage unless the config allows it and the user confirms.
- Broker keys live in environment variables or the Claude Desktop config, never in the chat.
